Ecosystems.intro: An ecosystem includes all the living organisms and non-living factors in an area. Understanding how ecosystems work and how organisms interact is fundamental to B7.

sections.title: Key Terms
points: Ecosystem — all living organisms (biotic) and non-living factors (abiotic) in an area
Population — all individuals of one species in an area
Community — all populations of different species in an area
Habitat — the place where an organism lives

sections.title: Abiotic and Biotic Factors
points: Abiotic (non-living): light intensity, temperature, moisture, pH, wind speed, CO₂ concentration
Biotic (living): predation, competition, disease, food availability

sections.title: Competition
points: Intraspecific — between individuals of the SAME species (most intense)
Interspecific — between individuals of DIFFERENT species
Resources competed for: food, water, space, light, mates

keyTerms.def: All living organisms and non-living factors in an area
Non-living factor affecting organisms (temperature, light, pH, etc.)
Living factor affecting organisms (predation, competition, disease)
All individuals of one species in an area

examTips: Know the difference between population (one species), community (all species) and ecosystem (+ abiotic factors).
Intraspecific competition is more intense than interspecific — competing for identical resources.
commonMistakes: Confusing community (living organisms only) with ecosystem (includes abiotic factors).
Forgetting abiotic factors — temperature, light, pH, moisture are all important.

Food Webs.intro: Food chains and food webs show feeding relationships between organisms. Energy flows through ecosystems from producers to consumers.

sections.title: Food Chains and Webs
points: Food chain shows ONE feeding pathway: producer → primary consumer → secondary consumer → tertiary consumer
Food web shows MULTIPLE interconnected food chains
Arrow direction = direction of energy transfer (NOT 'eaten by')
All food chains start with a PRODUCER (plant)

sections.title: Energy Transfer
points: Only about 10% of energy transfers between trophic levels
Energy lost as: heat (respiration), undigested material (faeces), movement
This explains why food chains are short (usually 4-5 levels max)
Biomass decreases at each level — shown by pyramid of biomass

callout.label: Pyramids
callout.text: Pyramid of biomass — always a true pyramid (wider at base). Pyramid of numbers can be unusual shape (e.g. many insects on one tree).

keyTerms.def: An organism that makes its own food by photosynthesis (plants, algae)
An organism that eats other organisms for energy
The position of an organism in a food chain
The total mass of living material at a trophic level

examTips: Arrows in food chains show direction of ENERGY FLOW not 'is eaten by'.
Only ~10% of energy passes between trophic levels — explain what happens to the other 90%.
commonMistakes: Drawing food chain arrows from consumer to producer ('X eats Y' direction).
Saying all pyramids of numbers are pyramid-shaped — they are NOT always pyramidal.

Nutrient Cycling.intro: Nutrients are constantly recycled through ecosystems. The carbon and water cycles are the main examples you need for GCSE Combined Science.

sections.title: The Carbon Cycle
points: Photosynthesis — removes CO₂ from atmosphere (carbon fixation)
Respiration — releases CO₂ back to atmosphere (all living things)
Decomposition — decomposers break down dead matter → CO₂ released
Combustion — burning fossil fuels and wood releases CO₂
Feeding — carbon passes along food chains

sections.title: The Water Cycle
points: Evaporation — water from surfaces enters atmosphere
Transpiration — water vapour released from plants
Condensation — water vapour cools and forms clouds
Precipitation — rain/snow returns water to land
Runoff/infiltration — water returns to rivers and groundwater

sections.title: Decomposers
points: Bacteria and fungi break down dead organic matter
Release mineral ions back into soil for plants
Release CO₂ and water through respiration
Essential for nutrient recycling — without them nutrients would be locked up in dead matter

keyTerms.def: The cycling of carbon through living organisms, the atmosphere and the Earth
Organism (bacteria/fungi) that breaks down dead material, recycling nutrients
Burning — releases stored carbon as CO₂

examTips: Decomposers release CO₂ through RESPIRATION — not photosynthesis.
Photosynthesis removes CO₂; respiration and combustion add it back.
The water cycle is driven by solar energy (evaporation) and gravity (precipitation).
commonMistakes: Forgetting combustion as a way CO₂ enters the atmosphere.

Decomposition.intro: Decomposition is the breakdown of dead organic matter by decomposers. It is essential for recycling nutrients back into ecosystems.

sections.title: Decomposers
points: Bacteria and fungi are the main decomposers
Break down dead plants and animals and animal waste
Release mineral ions into soil — available for plant uptake
Release CO₂ and water through respiration

sections.title: Factors Affecting Decomposition Rate
points: Temperature — higher temperature = faster decomposition (up to optimum — enzymes denature above ~40°C)
Moisture/water availability — more moisture = faster decomposition
Oxygen availability — aerobic decomposition faster than anaerobic
pH — neutral pH generally optimal

sections.title: Practical Applications
points: Composting — controlled decomposition of plant material; turning increases oxygen; warm conditions speed up
Sewage treatment — decomposers break down organic waste
Biogas — anaerobic decomposition produces methane (used as fuel)

keyTerms.def: The breakdown of dead organic matter by bacteria and fungi
Organism that breaks down dead organic material (bacteria and fungi)
Controlled aerobic decomposition of organic waste to produce compost

examTips: Decomposition is faster in warm, moist, aerobic conditions.
Decomposers respire — they use oxygen and produce CO₂ (in aerobic conditions).
Composting works better when turned regularly — increases oxygen supply.
commonMistakes: Forgetting that decomposers are bacteria AND fungi — not just bacteria.
Saying decomposition always needs oxygen — anaerobic decomposition also occurs (but is slower).

Biodiversity.intro: Biodiversity is the variety of living organisms in an ecosystem. High biodiversity is important for ecosystem stability and resilience.

sections.title: What is Biodiversity?
points: The variety of different species in an area
Also includes genetic diversity within species
High biodiversity = more stable ecosystem — if one species is lost, others can fill the role
Human activities have significantly reduced global biodiversity

sections.title: Why Biodiversity Matters
points: Food security — wild plants are source of new crop varieties
Medicines — many drugs derived from plants/animals
Ecosystem services — clean water, clean air, pollination, soil fertility
Intrinsic value — all species have a right to exist

callout.label: Species Richness vs Evenness
callout.text: Biodiversity considers both the NUMBER of different species AND how evenly distributed they are. High numbers of only one species does not mean high biodiversity.

keyTerms.def: The variety of different species in an ecosystem
The number of different species in an area
Benefits that humans receive from functioning ecosystems

examTips: High biodiversity = more stable ecosystem.
Biodiversity has been declining due to human activities — deforestation, pollution, overhunting.
Be able to suggest methods of preserving biodiversity.
commonMistakes: Thinking biodiversity just means lots of one species — it requires VARIETY of species.
Forgetting genetic diversity within species as part of biodiversity.

Climate Change.intro: Human activities are increasing greenhouse gas concentrations in the atmosphere, causing global warming and climate change with major ecological consequences.

sections.title: The Greenhouse Effect
points: Short-wave radiation from the Sun passes through the atmosphere
Earth's surface absorbs it and re-emits long-wave (infrared) radiation
Greenhouse gases (CO₂, methane, water vapour) absorb this — trapping heat
Natural greenhouse effect is essential for life; enhanced greenhouse effect = climate change

sections.title: Human Causes
points: Burning fossil fuels — releases CO₂ (electricity, transport, heating)
Deforestation — less photosynthesis; burning wood releases CO₂
Agriculture — cattle produce methane; rice paddies produce methane
Landfill — anaerobic decomposition produces methane

sections.title: Ecological Consequences
points: Rising sea levels — flooding of coastal habitats and human settlements
Changes in distribution of species — habitats shift towards poles
Disruption of ecosystems — timing of seasons, migration patterns, food availability altered
Extinction risk — species unable to adapt fast enough
Increased frequency of extreme weather events

keyTerms.def: Trapping of heat in the atmosphere by greenhouse gases
Rise in average global temperature due to enhanced greenhouse effect
Total amount of greenhouse gases produced by human activities

examTips: Be able to evaluate evidence for and against climate change — scientists use data from many sources.
Methane is a potent greenhouse gas — from livestock, landfill and rice paddies.
Climate change affects biodiversity — species unable to adapt quickly enough may go extinct.
commonMistakes: Confusing the greenhouse effect (natural process) with global warming (enhanced version causing climate change).
Saying the ozone hole causes climate change — they are separate issues.

Human Impact on Ecosystems.intro: Human activities have dramatically altered ecosystems worldwide. Understanding these impacts and ways to reduce them is important for B7.

sections.title: Deforestation
points: Removal of large areas of forest for agriculture, timber, development
Consequences: loss of habitat and biodiversity, release of stored carbon, less photosynthesis, soil erosion, disruption of water cycle
Particularly severe in tropical rainforests — enormous biodiversity

sections.title: Land Use Changes
points: Urbanisation — building on natural land removes habitats
Agriculture — monocultures reduce biodiversity; pesticides kill non-target species
Peat bogs drained — releases stored CO₂; destroys wetland habitat

sections.title: Pollution
points: Water pollution — eutrophication: fertiliser runoff → algal blooms → death of aquatic life
Air pollution — acid rain damages trees and soil chemistry
Plastic pollution — marine animals ingest or become entangled in plastic
Pesticides — accumulate in food chains (bioaccumulation)

sections.title: Conservation Methods
points: Breeding programmes for endangered species (e.g. zoos)
Habitat protection — national parks, nature reserves, marine conservation zones
Reforestation — replanting trees
Recycling and reducing waste
Sustainable fishing — quotas prevent overfishing
Reducing carbon emissions — renewable energy

keyTerms.def: Clearing large areas of forest, often for agriculture or development
Excess nutrients in water causing algal blooms and death of aquatic organisms
Build-up of toxins in organisms at higher trophic levels
Protection and management of natural environments and biodiversity

examTips: Eutrophication: fertiliser → algal bloom → algae die → bacteria decompose → use up O₂ → fish die.
Bioaccumulation: toxins concentrate at higher trophic levels — top predators most affected.
Be able to evaluate conservation methods — costs, benefits, and practicality.
commonMistakes: Confusing eutrophication stages — it's a chain of events, not just 'fertiliser kills fish'.
Forgetting that peat bogs are a carbon store — draining them releases CO₂.

Sampling.intro: Scientists use sampling techniques to estimate the size of populations and measure biodiversity without counting every individual.

sections.title: Quadrats
points: A square frame placed randomly in a habitat to count organisms within
Used for stationary organisms — plants, slow animals
Must be placed RANDOMLY to avoid bias — use random coordinates from a grid
Calculate population estimate: (count ÷ quadrat area) × total habitat area

sections.title: Transects
points: A line through a habitat along which samples are taken
Used to study how organisms change across a habitat gradient (e.g. from sea to inland)
Belt transect — quadrats placed at regular intervals along the line
Systematic sampling — not random, but positioned to capture gradients

sections.title: Mark-Release-Recapture
sections.text: Used to estimate the size of mobile animal populations.
numbered: Capture a sample, mark them (e.g. paint spot)
Release and allow to mix with population
Recapture a second sample, count marked individuals

callout.label: Lincoln Index Formula
callout.text: Population estimate = (first catch × second catch) ÷ number of marked individuals in second catch. Assumes: marks not lost/harmful, population closed (no births/deaths/migration).

keyTerms.def: A square frame used to sample stationary organisms in an area
A line through a habitat used to study distribution of organisms
Technique used to estimate the size of animal populations
Sampling with no pattern or bias — using random coordinates

examTips: Quadrats must be placed RANDOMLY — use random number coordinates to avoid bias.
Mark-release-recapture assumes marks don't affect survival, population doesn't change between catches.
Know the formula: population = (n1 × n2) ÷ m2
commonMistakes: Placing quadrats non-randomly (e.g. in nice-looking patches) — introduces bias.
Using mark-release-recapture for plants — they don't move! Use quadrats instead.
